rows.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `sep-2322-default-result-type-complete` / DefaultResultTypeComplete, decomposed by this ticket. It is the ONE case in this fixture where the client MUST NOT retry — so it looks like the counterpart, and the resemblance survives a careless read. Its antecedent is different: the failing arm is `if(t)` where `t` is `Client retried with inputResponses even though the result had no resultType`. The trigger is an ABSENT `resultType`, which the spec says defaults to `complete`; this claim's trigger is a resultType that explicitly SAYS `input_required` while the client has nothing configured to resolve it. And the fixture rules the declining client out from the other side: the scenario's `getChecks` seeds every unfired MRTR check `status:`FAILURE`` with `Tool was not called by client or MRTR flow not completed`, so a client that declines is scored as having failed the flow, never as having correctly declined. Both of the fixture's two `input_required` emissions ([345526] and [346965], measured) lead into a retry the checks then score.
rows.the_search_that_found_none: a client that receives an explicit `resultType: "input_required"` and has NO resolver configured, returning the result to its caller unchanged instead of retrying
rows.why_no_counterpart: `no-oc-fixture-case` — and this is the ONLY one of C1b-iii's 37 that is. The scenario EXISTS, is CLIENT-leg, is in this file's declared check population and is matched by five checks; what it has no case for is a client that declines to resolve. So the search is over the scenario's fixture bytes rather than over the 175.
rows.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is the declining client. S15's subject is that client, and the search is over the fixture that would have to contain such a case — the mock server the scenario's `start` builds. Its near miss, DefaultResultTypeComplete, is the one fixture case where the client must not retry, and its antecedent is different.

rows.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `MRTRClientParallelIsolation` — CLIENT-leg, in this file's declared check population, decomposed BY THIS TICKET, and its description is `inputRequests and requestState MUST NOT be used for any other request the client may be sending`. That is a check about a client with more than one request in flight, and the temptation to call it the counterpart is real. It is not one: its two axes are `unrelated_call_carries_no_input_responses` and `unrelated_call_carries_no_request_state`, both read off `e!==void 0` / `t!==void 0` at [347811,348009], and both are about MRTR state LEAKING between calls. This claim is about response CORRELATION and involves no MRTR flow at all, so it is not merely silent on the two axes — its subject is a different property of the same situation. That is why this is a bucket-1 record and not an all-silent edge: an all-silent edge says `there is a counterpart and our claim does not touch its predicate`, and here there is no counterpart to be silent about.

rows.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is response correlation under concurrency. S11's subject is that, and its near miss is the row a search on the obvious word returns — which is in this file's own declared check population and decomposed by this ticket, so the reason it is not a counterpart is stated against its axes rather than against its name.

rows.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `ServerSSEStreamsFunctional` — `Multiple POST SSE streams should be functional` — and it is a near miss a reader is very likely to stop at, because the harness genuinely pipes each stream through an SSE PARSER before reading it. It is still not a counterpart, and the decomposition of that check is what settles it: the stream is scored by racing ONE `read()` against a 2 second timer, and a `null` from the timer is not recorded as an error, so a stream whose frames are malformed enough to yield nothing is counted FUNCTIONAL exactly as one that delivers a frame. The event is never decoded and its payload is never compared with the request that opened it. So the check cannot distinguish correct framing from no framing at all, and nothing else in the 175 mentions an SSE field line. The second near miss is `SRV13`'s territory — the SSE response HEADERS — which is a different absence with its own entry and is named here only so the two are not confused.

rows.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is about the BYTES of an SSE frame. These are the nearest near miss in this whole file: the suite scores the `Mcp-Name` header on a tools/call, against `params.name`, which is word for word the pair this claim is about. AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS SOMETHING SHARPER THAN `NOT A COUNTERPART`. Read at the harness build rather than off the description, `checkMcpNameHeader` binds `i` to the body value and `a` to the header and reports on `a!==i` — a RAW string comparison, with no decoding anywhere in the 1793 bytes that hold both routing-header predicates end to end. It scores SUCCESS at the accepted run only because every tool name in the suite's fixture is header-safe and `encode_value/1` is therefore the identity on all of them. The suite has the check, its predicate could not score the decode, and its fixture never provokes the encode.
